content:
#1 Recently, Timothy Chow put out a question on MathOverflow asking if mathematicians can organize to use an alternative proof assistant that uses membership based set theory, instead of the currently dominant Lean that uses dependent type theory.

And this made me think that membership based set theory might be currently losing out on its former status as “the” foundations of mathematics, and that Timothy Chow and James Hanson’s efforts on MathOverflow are just a rear guard action for set theory proponents to keep membership based set theory like ZFC as the status as the foundations of mathematics that undergirds the entirety of mathematics. That is, if proof verification via proof assistants are part of the future of mathematics and Lean stays as the dominant one used in the mathematics community.

Edit: Timothy Chow made an comment to his question saying he personally has no preference between set theory vs type theory, but that other people in the mathematics community do have very strong preferences for set theory.

Edit 2: James Hanson made an answer saying that he cares more about user experience than foundational issues when it comes to proof assistants. When even an arch ZFC defender like James Hanson says he doesn’t really care about foundations in this case, philosophers of mathematics will have to figure out why foundational issues don’t matter to mathematicians as much as other concerns and mathematical values, considering they spent the past century making the foundations of mathematics the most important topic in the philosophy of mathematics alongside the ever recurring debates on realism vs nominalism.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#2 From the perspective of the philosophy of mathematics, this MathOverflow discussion really makes it seem like the question of foundations to be more sociological in nature than anything intrinsic about the nature of mathematical objects. People base their identities on membership based set theory being “the” foundations of mathematics since the early 1900s, and are upset that more and more people think differently in the 21st century.

On the other hand, I also don’t think that the type theorists will “win” either and replace set theory as the dominant foundations of mathematics; rather it seems like the future is going to be a pluralist land where multiple foundations coexist with each other. All the set theory membership notation in mathematics textbooks won’t go away. Maybe the only requirement in the future is that you need to have some form of the basic axioms in your theory, such as power sets, natural numbers / infinity, replacement, choice, and extensionality in your foundations.

Maybe in the future foundations will also be acknowledged to merely be theoretical models for how general mathematical objects / collections behave, rather than the vaulted status it holds in mathematics and the philosophy of mathematics it currently has.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#3 Relatedly, a huge topic in the foundations in recent years is whether foundations should accept large cardinal axioms. Proof assistants like Lean, Agda, Rocq, etc all answer the question in the affirmative, yes mathematics should have large cardinal axioms in the foundations. The future default for people who use set theory might not be ZFC, but rather something like ZFC + Mahlo cardinals.

The large cardinal axioms in set theory and universe hierarchies in type theory are a reason why for the longest time I didn’t like any of these proof assistants (since large cardinals / universes just didn’t exist in ZFC and ETCS and related set theories), but if they become accepted throughout mathematics maybe I might have to change my mind.

Edit: There’s another MathOverflow question here with some discussion about how Lean is equivalent to strength to ZFC + large cardinal axioms and can be used to prove the consistency of ZFC, and how that can be used as an argument against using Lean for people who want to keep mathematics = anything provable from within ZFC. Some quotes:

  • from Timothy Chow:

Finally, if you’re the kind of person who worries about the fundamental axioms of mathematics, you might like to know that the consistency of the type theory underlying Lean cannot be proved in ZFC alone; you need a weak large cardinal axiom. For more details, see The Type Theory of Lean (Mario Carneiro again).

  • from Gro-Tsen:

The foundational basis on which Lean rests may differ from the ones we expect (say, first-order ZFC): i.e., at the purely logical level, a theorem in Lean is not the same as a theorem in ZFC, because they have different axioms, and even for first-order arithmetical statement they will likely differ. I do not know the details of Lean, but if its type theory is powerful enough, it seems plausible to me that Lean might prove “ZFC is consistent”: if this is the case, “ZFC is consistent” is an arithmetical statement that Lean proves and ZFC doesn’t, so we cannot blindly accept as ZFC theorems anything Lean declares as valid (of course, there’s nothing magical about first-order ZFC, so maybe one can argue that Lean makes a better foundation for mathematics, but this requires at least a rethinking of mathematical orthodoxy).

Large cardinals alone seem like they’re going to reopen the foundations debate that’s been closed off to the mathematical mainstream since the 1930s.

Probably the person I would be most interested to see the reaction to all this is Penelope Maddy; if she’s going to deal with the rise of the use of Lean and dependent type theory among mathematicians and what that means for set theory as a privileged foundations of mathematics. This is made all the more important because Lean is stronger than ZFC since it implies the consistency of ZFC, and a big part of her recent work in the foundations is finding new axiom candidates such as large cardinal axioms that one can add to ZFC / the foundations of mathematics. Lean and other dependent type theories with their universe hierarchies are likely going to have a bigger impact on this question of new axioms for set theory than the stuff happening at the frontiers of membership based set theory like V = L.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#4 On an almost converse note:

It’s tragic, or at least anti-climactic, that Lean:

(1.) comes onto the scene as a HoTT prover (Lean 2)

(2.) drops the HoTT support (Lean 3)

(3.) becomes hugely popular.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#5 I’d say that it’s actually better for the wider adoption of dependent type theory among mathematicians that Lean 3 made its decision to get rid of HoTT and just squashed all the identity types to strict propositions. Switching from membership based set theory to a dependent type theory where all types are h-sets is already a significant shift in thinking about sets that mathematicians have to get used to; I don’t think the average mathematician needs to also be burdened by having to think about transporting elements of identity types everywhere. It’s a lot easier to jump from ZFC to Lean and then Lean to HoTT than it is to jump straight from ZFC to HoTT.

Lean could have easily remained as a HoTT prover and then mathematicians could have easily adopted something like Isabelle/ZF as their choice of proof assistant and continued to ignore dependent type theory.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#6 Proof assistants, combined with LLMs proving or refuting theorems, are likely going to force a paradigm shift in the philosophy of mathematics where they now have to focus on what mathematicians actually value and practice, rather than what they idealise. Along the way, philosophers of mathematics may shift to an anti-foundationalist point of view and end up concluding that 20th century philosophy of mathematics is largely a dead end because it focused too much on the foundations of mathematics to the exclusion of everything else, philosophical issues which in hindsight not many mathematicians really cared about in practice. 21st century philosophy of mathematics might be more influenced by Lakatos than the likes of Frege, Russell, Hilbert, etc.

This is especially the case if the prediction that pure mathematics doesn’t have much of a future in academia, as discussed in the nForum discussion about the nLab during the era of LLMs, ends up becoming true. When the only mathematicians proving theorems are hobbyists outside of academia, the philosophy of mathematics as theorem proving and the foundations of mathematics both become about as important as the philosophy of artisan crafts that have been obsoleted by the industrial revolution in the 19th century.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants

content:
#7 RE: large cardinal axioms.

The relevant large cardinal axiom here is the axiom which say there exists a countably infinite number of inaccessible cardinals.

Now about the history of inaccessible cardinals: the relevant notion of inaccessible cardinal here is that of a strongly inaccessible cardinal. Strongly inaccessible cardinals were only defined in 1930 by Zermeo, Sierpiński, and Tarski. Already this was around the time when ZFC was accepted as the foundations of mathematics, so inaccessible cardinals barely missed the boat. Moreover, inaccessible cardinals didn’t find use in mathematics until the 1950s with the advent of category theory, in the guise of Grothendieck universes, and later in the 1970s to address paradoxes in type theory like Girard’s paradox, in the guise of the universe hierarchy. Most of the rest of mathematics initially didn’t have need for inaccessible cardinals, so they were just content with assuming ZFC.

Only now, with the mainstreaming of category theory and type theory into the rest of mathematics, do we perhaps have the need to add inaccessible cardinals to ZFC and inaccessible sets to ETCS for the foundations of mathematics.

content: #10 And even so, the ‘countably-infinite number of inaccessibles’ needed for the type theory here is not really the same as in say ZFC+etc. The index parameter for the universes is not a set/type like ω\omegaω of N\mathbb{N}N, but a very weak meta-theoretic structure that only captures a decidable fragment of arithmetic: you need 0 and max{n,m} and maybe successor. It’s a very narrow distinction, but it’s important from the point of view of actual implementation of a proof assistant.
subject: Foundations of mathematics and proof assistants
